title: Galen cites On the Elements according to Hippocrates and Causes of Symptoms
summary: For his account of how pain arises Galen refers to two of his own works, On the Elements according to Hippocrates and the Causes of Symptoms.
quote: it has been stated by me both in the work On the Elements according to Hippocrates
note: Galen's De elementis ex Hippocrate and De symptomatum causis. The draft points out that the Greek title has its words in a disturbed order.

title: Galen contrasts his useful exegesis with other commentators' sophistry
summary: Galen says other exegetes fill their commentaries with sophistical questions that are useless for practice. He chooses instead to add useful teaching that follows from Hippocrates' doctrines.
quote: for they sow their exegeses with sophistical questions that are of no use to learners toward the end of the art

title: Barley or bitter-vetch fomentation: pound, boil in oxycrate, bag
summary: Galen explains that the barley and bitter vetch of Hippocrates' fomentation are pounded before being boiled in vinegar and water and sewn into bags. Bran is prepared the same way, and bitter vetch cuts thick humours.
quote: Both barley and bitter vetch he bids one boil in vinegar and water not as whole seeds, but having first pounded them
note: The lemma says the vinegar mixture should be 'a little sharper than one would drink it'. In K15.524-525 Galen explains this middle strength: inflamed parts cannot bear pungent oxycrate.

title: Anatomical Procedures book III and Anatomy of Veins and Arteries
summary: On the elbow veins cut in venesection Galen refers to the third book of his Anatomical Procedures and to a separate single book on the anatomy of veins and arteries.
quote: these have been sufficiently discussed both in the third book of the Anatomical Procedures and in the Anatomy of the Veins and Arteries, written separately in another single book
note: De anatomicis administrationibus III and De venarum arteriarumque dissectione.

title: Azygos vein origin differs between animals and humans
summary: Galen says the unpaired vein that feeds the lower eight ribs branches off above the heart in some animals. In others, humans included, it branches off where the vena cava meets the right auricle.
quote: a single unpaired (azygos) vein, which in some animals grows off above the heart
note: This comparative anatomy comes from Galen's own dissections.

title: Colour change of blood as limit of venesection
summary: Blood is let until its colour changes: redder if the body's blood is phlegmatic, livid or blackish if it is red. If the patient's strength cannot bear that much, Galen says it is better to stop than to break down the faculty.
quote: it is more fitting to refrain from breaking down the faculty than from evacuating the excess blood

title: Aromatic seeds added to purgatives to protect stomach mouth
summary: Fragrant additives are mixed with black hellebore or peplion (daucus, seseli, cumin, anise, silphium juice) so that the purgative does not touch the sensitive mouth of the stomach unmixed.
quote: the admixture of the aromatic substances was devised, so that the power of the purgative drugs might not touch the mouth of the stomach by itself and unmixed
note: The lemma (K15.535-536) lists the additives. This unit's checks verdict is 'fail'.

title: Purgatives known by experience, need for purging by reason
summary: Galen refers to his books On the Power of Simple Drugs: which humour a purgative draws is learned by experience, while the need to purge downward-tending humours was found by reason and confirmed by experience.
quote: That the cathartic drugs are discovered through experience—both which humour each purges and whether it purges at all—you have learned in the books on the power of simple drugs
note: This is the De simplicium medicamentorum temperamentis ac facultatibus.

title: Hiera made with colocynth; best version has hellebore, no scammony
summary: Among purgatives Galen names the colocynth preparation that people now call hiera. Of its several versions he judges best the one that contains hellebore but no scammony.
quote: among which is also the one made with colocynth, which they now customarily call hiera.
note: K15.540 continues: 'the one that has received hellebore but does not contain scammony is the finest drug'.

title: Contemporary physicians overfeed after evacuation
summary: Galen says most physicians of his day feed patients abundantly after evacuating them. Hippocrates gives less ptisan after purging, because the exhausted faculty cannot work up much food.
quote: For these, whenever they have evacuated, feed abundantly

title: Physicians dry patients out 'like salt-fish' before feeding
summary: Galen attacks physicians who starve patients for two or three days at the start of a disease and then switch abruptly to gruels. He compares this to pickling fish.
quote: as if curing them like salt-fish, for two or three days or even more
note: In K15.594-595 Galen glosses ταριχεύεσθαι as excessive drying from untimely fasting.

title: Aristotelians call self-evident premises 'axioms'
summary: Analysing Hippocrates' argument as a syllogism, Galen notes that the followers of Aristotle call premises credible in themselves 'axioms'.
quote: which premises it is in fact the custom of the followers of Aristotle to call axioms

title: Asian Greeks still say 'greenish' for pale-yellow
summary: To explain Hippocrates' 'greenish' urine, Galen cites a usage still current among the Greeks of Asia. They call a sallow person chlōros, using it the same as ōchros.
quote: by 'greenish' he speaks according to a certain usage of the Greeks in Asia, which is preserved even now
note: This is evidence for spoken Greek in Galen's home region of Asia Minor.

title: Accent of ōchra (ochre) noted
summary: Galen defines the pale-yellow colour by the pigment ochre and notes that the word is accented with an acute on the first syllable.
quote: such as that of what is called ōchra (ochre), the name being accented with an acute on the first syllable

title: Variant reading spatilē versus asē
summary: Galen reports that many copies of Hippocrates read asē (restless distress) instead of spatilē (liquid stool). He explains what each reading would mean.
quote: but in many of the copies you will find written not spatilē [556] but asē (restless distress)

title: Most commentators read 'sleep after dinner'; Galen says after lunch
summary: Galen disagrees with most earlier commentators, who took the advice to sleep 'as if passing the night' to mean after dinner. He argues from the context that it means after the midday meal and offers an emendation.
quote: after dinner, as most of the commentators say, but, as the sense of what has been said requires, after the midday meal
note: In K15.557-558 he gives the corrected wording, 'one must sleep... after the luncheon'.

title: Paulus the rhetor: phlegmatic, vomited yellow bile daily
summary: Galen's example of a man 'bitter-bilious in the upper parts' is Paulus the rhetor. He had a phlegmatic habit of body, yet yellow bile rose every day and he vomited it after his bath, and his stools held little bile.
quote: For in Paulus the rhetor, who had a phlegmatic habit of the whole body, yellow bile floated up every day, and he vomited it first, after the bath, in no small quantity.
note: This passage does not identify him further. He is distinct from the Eudemus case that follows.

title: Eudemus the philosopher: bilious, bile passed downward
summary: The contrasting case is Eudemus the philosopher. He was bilious in temperament, his bile passed downward, he rarely vomited it, and his stools were full of bile.
quote: But in Eudemus the philosopher, who was bilious in temperament, it passed downward through the seat
note: Most likely the Peripatetic Eudemus whom Galen treated in Rome (On Prognosis).

title: Stool frequency of Eudemus versus Paulus
summary: Galen reports that Eudemus went to stool two or three times a day, while Paulus sometimes passed nothing at all. He explains this by where each man's bile went.
quote: Hence Eudemus went to stool twice each day, and sometimes even three times, whereas Paulus at times did not excrete at all.

title: Bile duct sometimes has a branch into the stomach
summary: Galen explains why yellow bile rises in some people: the duct from the liver to the outgrowth of the stomach is built differently in some, with a branch reaching the stomach.
quote: For sometimes in some people a branch from it reaches the stomach; in these, then, the bilious residue floats up above
note: This is an anatomical variant of the bile duct based on dissection.

title: Synkomistos bread now called autopyros
summary: Hippocrates' synkomistos bread, made with the bran left in, is what people of Galen's day call autopyros.
quote: people nowadays call such bread autopyros, since the branny flour in it is not separated out but is kneaded up together with the pure

title: Potainia: Ionic word for fresh barley-groats
summary: Galen notes that Hippocrates calls fresh barley-groats potainia, in the dialect of the Ionians and the older writers.
quote: he called the fresh ones potainia in the dialect of the Ionians and of the older writers

title: Empiricist 'syndromes' cannot capture degrees of illness
summary: Galen argues that teaching by the Empiricists' syndromes cannot work, because the degrees of strength, fever and sputum cannot be written down. The physician has to weigh them himself in each case.
quote: it is not possible to conduct the teaching according to what the Empiricists call syndromes.

title: Therapeutic Method gives the orderly teaching Hippocrates lacked
summary: Galen refers readers to his Therapeutic Method for the ordered treatment of quantity of food. He excuses Hippocrates' disorder because Hippocrates was the first to discover these things.
quote: All such matters have been stated in the treatise on the therapeutic method, in sequence and in order
note: This is the Methodus medendi.

title: Part 'after the bath' published posthumously from Hippocrates' notes
summary: Galen suggests that the section after the bath may be notes Hippocrates wrote for himself, found in his house and published after his death. As a treatise it is unworthy of him, like On Diseases and On Affections.
quote: if someone, having found it in the house, published it after the man's death as things written by him in outline
note: This is the so-called Appendix to Regimen in Acute Diseases.

title: Galen promises commentaries on On Diseases and On Affections
summary: Galen says he will settle whether On Diseases and On Affections are authentic in commentaries written on those works.
quote: we shall define this same point and decide it in the commentaries written on them
note: No Galenic commentaries on these works survive. They may have been planned only or are lost.

title: Books On Difficulty of Breathing cited
summary: Galen refers to his books On Dyspnoea, where he set out the causes of all kinds of laboured breathing with demonstrations.
quote: in which we have written out the causes both of these and of the other dyspnoeas together with their proper demonstrations
note: This is De difficultate respirationis in three books. It is cited again at K15.793-794.

title: Prognostic, On Humours and Aphorisms commentaries written earlier
summary: Galen says that before this commentary he had already expounded the Prognostic, On Humours and the Aphorisms. He also refers to his books On Crises.
quote: For we have already expounded, before this book, both the Prognostic and the work On Humours and the Aphorisms
note: This is evidence for the relative order of Galen's Hippocratic commentaries.

title: Layman who feeds a starved patient seems to raise the dead
summary: If a physician fails to see that a patient is weak from starvation, another physician or a layman who feeds him looks as if he had raised a dead man. Galen says such errors bring the craft into contempt.
quote: for the physician or layman who came in seems to them as if he had even raised up a dead man.

title: Reading anōterō versus exōterō argued letter by letter
summary: Against interpreters who take 'still earlier' as days 7 to 9, Galen argues that they would then have to write ἐξωτέρω, with epsilon and xi, not ἀνωτέρω.
quote: these people ought, if this was what pleased them, to write the beginning of the word with the letters epsilon and xi, ἐξωτέρω, and not ἀνωτέρω with alpha and nu.
note: This unit's checks verdict is 'fail'.

title: Book found in drafts; notes on front and back of sheet
summary: Galen explains the book's disorder: it was found in draft form after Hippocrates' death. Examples he added on the front and back of the sheet were put in the wrong places by the copyist.
quote: the examples that he had found were written in addition into the book by Hippocrates himself, for the confirmation of the universal statement, some on the front of the sheet and some on the back
note: The Greek is ἐπὶ τοῦ μετώπου / κατὰ τοῦ νώτου. This is evidence for ancient ideas about how texts were transmitted. Checks verdict is 'fail'.

title: Five differences of wine: colour, taste, consistency, smell, power
summary: Galen faults Hippocrates' list of wines as disordered and incomplete and sets out five kinds of difference. The colours are white, black, tawny, yellow and red.
quote: another is the quality according to taste, a third according to consistency, a fourth according to smell, and a fifth according to power.

title: Theraean and Scybelite: outstandingly sweet, thick, black wines
summary: Galen's examples of sweet wines are the Theraean and the Scybelite, both thick and black.
quote: At any rate the Theraean and the Scybelite are sweet wines to an outstanding degree, both being thick and black

title: Maeonian sweet wines: Therinos and Karyinos
summary: Sweet wines are also made in Maeonia, the Therinos and the Karyinos. They are less sweet, thick and black than the Theraean and the Scybelite.
quote: sweet too are those produced in Maeonia, the Therinos and the Karyinos

title: Hepsēma and siraion: boiled-down must
summary: Galen describes hepsēma and siraion, made by boiling down must. The sweeter it becomes, the blacker and thicker it is, and over-boiled must turns bitter.
quote: what is called hepsēma and siraion, which is produced from must being boiled down
note: K15.632-633 adds that must boiled too long turns bitter, as honey does.

title: Cough as a 'hand'; viscous phlegm clings like birdlime
summary: Galen says the breath of a cough acts like a hand that carries thick humours up, but viscous humours stick in the bronchi like birdlime. So melikraton suits thick sputa and oxymel viscous ones.
quote: And for this reason melikraton is most suitable for the thick humours with a view to expectoration, and oxymel for the viscous ones

title: Greek terms stryphnos (harsh) versus austēros (dry) wine
summary: Galen notes that the Greeks call an excessively astringent wine stryphnos and a more moderate one austēros.
quote: which the Greeks also call stryphnos (harsh), while they call the more moderate one austēros (dry)

title: Dark austere wines near Pergamum, Perperina and Aegae
summary: Not all dark wines are sweet. Galen's examples are the austere dark wines of his home region in Asia, near Pergamum and around Perperina and Aegae.
quote: some of them are austere, such as those among us in Asia near Pergamum and around Perperina and Aegae.
note: Checks verdict is 'fail'.

title: Cilician Anabates wine: sweet and austere at once, bad
summary: Galen says the Anabates of Cilicia combines austere and sweet qualities. For that reason it is a bad wine that lingers in the upper belly and causes wind.
quote: The Anabates in Cilicia is at once both austere and sweet, being compounded of opposite qualities
note: Checks verdict is 'fail'.

title: Watery wines for fever patients: Sabine, Titacazene, Tibine
summary: The best wine for the feverish is watery, white, thin and odourless. Galen's examples are the slack Sabine of Italy, which is given to fever patients, and the Titacazene and Tibine of Asia.
quote: in Italy the slack Sabine, which they also give to those with fever; in Asia the Titacazene and the Tibine.

title: Galen found watery wines in Cilicia, Phoenicia, Palestine, Scyros, Crete, Egypt
summary: Galen says he found thin watery wines in Cilicia, Phoenicia, Palestine, Scyros and Crete, and even in Egypt, though hot regions usually make thick strong wines. In Italy, Bithynia and Asia such wines are common.
quote: I at any rate have found wines of this kind in Cilicia and Phoenicia and Palestine and Scyros and Crete
note: This is evidence for Galen's travels (compare his journeys to Palestine and Cyprus mentioned in Simple Drugs). Checks verdict is 'fail'.

title: Sykota: fig-fattened livers
summary: To show that the viscera delight in sweet things, Galen points to the so-called sykota: livers that grow very large and delicious when the animal is fed dried figs.
quote: the so-called sykota (fig-fed livers) are seen, through the eating of dried figs, to become very large and most delicious
note: This is the ancient forerunner of foie gras (iecur ficatum).

title: Frothy, intensely bilious stools mean colliquative fever: stop melikraton
summary: Frothy, intensely bilious stools show that the fever is colliquative. Galen says to stop melikraton, move to ptisan juice, and give cold water at the right moment for the greatest benefit.
quote: know that the fever is colliquative, and on this account desist from the use of melikraton and proceed to the juice of ptisane

title: Sinea: Ionic for 'harms'; shown in On Fractures/Joints commentary
summary: Galen explains Hippocrates' σίνεα: the Ionians say sinein for blaptein, 'to injure'. He says he showed this in his commentary on On Fractures and On Joints.
quote: for indeed the Ionians say sinein in place of blaptein ("to injure")
note: The draft's 'treatise On Fractures and On Joints' refers to Galen's commentaries on those works.

title: Melikraton can stretch survival from four days to five or six
summary: Melikraton is not a weakener but a light nourishment. Galen says a fasting man who would die in four days could reach the fifth or sixth on melikraton.
quote: if someone who had fasted were going to die in four days, this person, using melikraton, could arrive not only at the fifth day but even at the sixth.
note: This answers the lemma (K15.665) that melikraton got a reputation for causing swift death through people who starved themselves to death on it.

title: Raw melikraton more laxative, boiled more nourishing
summary: As a side note Galen says raw melikraton loosens the bowels more, while well-boiled melikraton nourishes more.
quote: raw melikraton is more laxative, while that which has been well boiled is more nourishing

title: Dosage test: one kyathos of honey versus two of wine daily
summary: To compare the nourishment in honey and wine fairly, Galen describes a trial: one kyathos of honey a day against two kyathoi of wine, each diluted as the patient likes.
quote: he can, say, take one kyathos of honey either by itself or, mixing in as much water as he wishes
note: The kyathos is about 0.045 litre.

title: Oxymel is melikraton with a little vinegar, best boiled
summary: Galen says proper oxymel is not simply vinegar and honey but melikraton with a small amount of vinegar. Boiling it is better, because boiling weakens the vinegar's harm while keeping its benefit.
quote: For the composition of oxymel does not come about merely from a mixture of vinegar and honey, but from melikraton that takes on a small quantity of vinegar.

title: Holding back stool when no privy is near
summary: Galen illustrates reverse peristalsis from ordinary life. When we hold back a bowel movement because of urgent business or because no privy is near, we feel the bile run back up.
quote: or because there is no privy near at hand; for on such occasions we perceive the bile running back up in such a way that it is no longer excreted.
note: The same unit cites his commentaries On the Natural Faculties for peristalsis.

title: Anatomists by autopsy call the womb sinewy; hence vinegar harms it
summary: Vinegar harms sinewy parts. Nearly all anatomists, from dissection, call the womb sinewy, and Galen adds that its huge range of dilation proves it.
quote: nearly all the anatomists say that the womb is sinewy
note: This explains the lemma (K15.692-693) that vinegar is hostile to women because it pains the womb.

title: Erasistratus' dictum on strong powers of food and drink
summary: Galen quotes Erasistratus: strong foods and drinks bring the greatest benefit at the right moment and the greatest harm at the wrong one. He uses it to explain why physicians fall back on water.
quote: for so Erasistratus used to say: strong powers of foods and drinks, when taken at the right moment, bring the greatest benefit, but when at the wrong moment, the greatest harm.

title: Old man on watery wine; rival mocks 'he only looks at it'
summary: Galen tells how he gave a sick old man water with a few drops of wine each day. A visiting physician laughed that the patient was not drinking wine but only looking at it. Galen explains that wine given for benefit is mixed differently from wine given for pleasure.
quote: laughed and said that the sick man was not drinking wine [699] but only looking at it
note: Checks verdict is 'fail'.

title: Erasistratus' On Fevers mocks Hippocrateans' wax cups
summary: Galen says Erasistratus, in his books On Fevers, maliciously attacks Hippocrates through his pupils Apollonius and Dexippus. They supposedly made wax cups of one twelfth of a kyathos and gave fever patients one or two of them.
quote: having made twelve waxen cyathi to the cyathus that is the sixth part of the cotyle, measured out one or two of these to those suffering from fever.
note: This is a fragment of Erasistratus' lost On Fevers. It also gives a measure: the kyathos is one sixth of a kotyle. K15.744 calls these 'wax cups' (κηρίνων κυλίκων).

title: Apollonius and Dexippus, pupils of Hippocrates
summary: Apollonius and Dexippus are named as Hippocrates' pupils who restricted drink in fevers. Galen says Erasistratus could produce no book of theirs.
quote: Erasistratus, who mentions Apollonius and Dexippus while having no book of theirs to show
note: Dexippus of Cos is known from other sources (for example Plutarch) as a pupil of Hippocrates.

title: Hippocratic treatments of individual acute diseases lost or never written
summary: Galen says Hippocrates' books on treating each acute disease either do not survive or were never written. Those in circulation are not worthy of him, though they contain much of his thought.
quote: It is therefore evident either that the books written by him on the treatment of each of the acute diseases in particular are not preserved, or that they were not written at all

title: No public bath-houses in Hippocrates' time
summary: From Hippocrates' remarks about house equipment, smokeless shelter and plentiful water, Galen infers that bath-houses had not yet been built. Water was still heated in cauldrons at home and poured into tubs.
quote: It seems that in the times of Hippocrates these bath-houses had not yet been constructed
note: This is evidence for ancient views on the history of the bath.

title: Bathing in tubs in army camps without a bathhouse
summary: Galen notes that patients are still often bathed in a room with a fire and a tub of water in army camps, wherever there is no bathhouse.
quote: which even now often happens in army camps, whenever someone needs to bathe but the place has no bathhouse

title: Low pools at natural springs, level with the floor
summary: The easiest tub to get in and out of is like the pools at natural hot springs. These are built so low that they hardly rise above the surrounding floor.
quote: best and least fatiguing of all is the arrangement in the bathing-pools at natural waters, which nearly everyone makes so low that they do not project at all above the adjoining floor

title: After the bath: three graded lukewarm affusions
summary: Healthy people plunge into cold water after the hot bath, but the sick cannot bear it. Galen advises at least three lukewarm waters, each cooler than the last, poured over the patient.
quote: those will do better who prepare no fewer than three lukewarm waters for after the hot bath, differing from one another
note: K15.710-711 says physicians of Galen's day pour lukewarm water instead of using the cold basin.

title: Modern practice: no strigil; patients wrapped in linen or unfulled cloaks
summary: Galen reports that physicians of his day use neither strigil nor sponge on the sick. After the bath they wrap them in linen or in cloaks, especially unfulled ones, to make them sweat.
quote: Nor do physicians nowadays use strigils on the sick, nor indeed a sponge either, but after the bath they wrap them in a linen cloth

title: Physician's book for Victor, prefect of Rome, excerpted Hippocrates
summary: Galen says a physician gave Victor, the prefect of Rome, a book On Regimen according to Hippocrates. It included this passage and others, though some of them cut in half.
quote: the physician who gave [723] to Victor, the prefect of Rome, the book On Regimen according to Hippocrates
note: Victor is a city prefect (praefectus urbi), possibly Aufidius Victorinus (city prefect under Commodus). The identification is uncertain. The book is a lost contemporary Hippocratic compilation.

title: Dogmatist versus Empiricist readings of Hippocrates against the Cnidians
summary: Those who think Hippocrates was a Dogmatist say he meant affected places, conditions and causes. Those who think him an Empiricist say seasons, regions, ages, habits and air. Galen accepts both but says this book uses other indications.
quote: Those who consider Hippocrates to be a Dogmatist said that these things are the affected places and their conditions and the causes

title: Interpolators insert at the ends of treatises
summary: Galen explains that interpolations cluster at the ends of books because readers remember the beginnings. He gives as examples the Aphorisms, On Wounds in the Head and Epidemics II, as well as this book.
quote: For because the first parts of treatises are in the memory of many, those who interpolate insert their interpolations into the last parts

title: Appendix perhaps by a pupil, or Hippocrates' preparatory notes
summary: Physicians suspected the section after the baths. Galen says its thought fits Hippocrates, so a pupil may have written it, or Hippocrates may have written it in preparing the promised book on each acute disease.
quote: so that one would suspect that some pupil of his wrote it.

title: Galen's own thirst worsened by strong old wine after a summer walk
summary: Galen recalls that once, thirsty from a summer journey on foot, he drank a single cup of old, rather strongly mixed wine. It increased his thirst rather than quenching it.
quote: I myself, at any rate, know that once, having become thirsty from a summer journey on foot, and then having drunk a single cup of old wine that was a little too strongly mixed

title: Burning fever from wine mixed with sea-water and salted foods
summary: Galen knows people seized by kausos after drinking a lot of wine mixed with sea-water, and others after eating too much salt-fish, salted meat and other salty foods.
quote: I know of some who were seized by burning fever because of drinking a rather large quantity of wine mixed with sea-water
note: Wine treated with sea-water was a known style, for example Coan.

title: Burning fever after bath plus strong wine, anger or sleeplessness
summary: A man came home from a hot journey on foot, bathed, then drank wine with a high wine-to-water ratio and fell straight into burning fever. Others fell ill after violent anger or sleeplessness.
quote: Another man, coming from a journey on foot and from burning heat, first bathed, and then, having arrived [740] home and drunk wine which had the larger share in the mixture
note: Checks verdict is 'fail'.

title: Appendix already attached by Erasistratus' time
summary: Even if the appendix is not by Hippocrates, Galen says it is ancient and was already joined to the genuine part in Erasistratus' day. That makes Erasistratus' mockery of the wax cups all the stranger.
quote: This book, even if it is not a composition of Hippocrates, is at any rate ancient, so that already in the times of Erasistratus it had been appended to the genuine part.
note: This dates the joining of Acut. and Appendix before about 250 BC.

title: Separating whey from ass's milk with a cold bronze vessel
summary: Instead of whole boiled ass's milk, Galen suggests using the whey alone. The milk is boiled with oxymel and a bronze vessel full of cold water is lowered into it again and again, which separates the whey from the curd.
quote: once you have first boiled the milk with oxymel, by repeatedly lowering into the milk a bronze vessel full of cold water

title: Pungent substances: pepper, mustard, pellitory (Simple Drugs IV)
summary: Galen cites book IV of On Simple Drugs: pepper, mustard, pellitory and other hot substances taste pungent. Salty things dry even more than pungent ones but heat less.
quote: pepper and mustard and pellitory, and all the other things that are hot in their powers, also appear pungent to those who taste them

title: Causi resolved by parotid swellings, but not genuine causi
summary: Galen says resolution of kausos through an abscess is extremely rare. He knows cases resolved by parotid swellings, but they were not genuine causi.
quote: For I know of some causi that were judged by parotid swellings, but not the genuine ones

title: Cold water in causus: Galen claims no deaths, too many to count
summary: Galen calls cold water the most powerful remedy for kausos. He says none of the patients he gave it to at the proper moment died, and they were too many to remember. In K15.753 he adds that he did not give it to hopeless cases.
quote: upon all to whom I gave it—and they are so very many that I do not even remember their number—there followed both benefit and preservation.

title: Galen refuses to divine 'attractive gruels'
summary: Galen admits he cannot tell what the author means by 'attractive gruels', since neither oxymel nor ptisan draws anything. He declines to guess and censures fondness for obscure expressions.
quote: am unable to divine what he can possibly mean by "attractive gruels"

title: Two books by Galen on phlebotomy
summary: Galen says the most persuasive views on venesection are set out in two of his books. One is titled On Phlebotomy and teaches everything useful; the other was written for physicians, Empiricists and Dogmatists.
quote: the one of them is entitled On Phlebotomy, in which everything useful is taught; the other has been written, as I said, for the physicians, both the Empiricists and the Dogmatists
note: These are probably De curandi ratione per venae sectionem and one of the anti-Erasistratean venesection books. The description of the second book ('as I said', 'for the physicians') is odd and may be corrupt.

title: Thessalian Methodists: phlebotomy as a 'relaxing' remedy
summary: Galen says the 'unmethodical Thessalians' declare phlebotomy a relaxing remedy without demonstration and explain 'relaxing' in different ways. He has examined this in his commentaries on the Methodic sect.
quote: But the unmethodical Thessalians, just as they state everything else [764] simply and without demonstration, so too have declared phlebotomy to be a relaxing remedy
note: The Thessalians are the followers of Thessalus of Tralles. The phrase 'unmethodical' (ἀμέθοδοι) is a pun on 'Methodists'.

title: Galen's commentaries on the Methodic sect
summary: Galen refers to his own commentaries examining the Methodic sect.
quote: as has been shown by me in my commentaries when examining the Methodic sect
note: This is perhaps the lost work in six books On the Methodic Sect (listed in On His Own Books).

title: Children and old men not bled; children's evacuation is innate
summary: The indications for phlebotomy are magnitude of disease, strength and prime age. Children are not bled because their moist, hot temperament disperses their substance, and old men are not bled because of weakness.
quote: they therefore have no need of phlebotomy, since they possess as something innate the evacuation that arises from their temperament.

title: Menodotus the Empiricist: bleed only in plethoric syndrome
summary: Galen reports that Menodotus the Empiricist held venesection appropriate only in the 'plethoric syndrome'. Galen bleeds also for sudden violent pain, bruises and dislocations, and sometimes treats plethora without bleeding.
quote: among whom is also Menodotus the Empiricist, who asserts that phlebotomy has been observed to apply only in the so-called plethoric concurrence
note: Menodotus of Nicomedia, Empiricist, 2nd century AD. This is a fragment of his views.

title: Plethora reduced without bleeding in two or three days
summary: Even when the plethoric syndrome is present Galen does not always bleed. Rubbing, more frequent baths and a reduced diet restore the patient in two or three days. He refers to On Plethora, On Phlebotomy and the Therapeutic Method.
quote: by means of rubbing and more frequent baths and a deficient regimen we bring the patient back to the natural state in two or even three days

title: Phlegmone's old broad sense; Galen's book on swellings
summary: In Hippocrates phlegmainein covered all hot swellings (erysipelas, herpes, anthrax), while recent physicians restrict it. Oedema too once meant any swelling. Galen refers to his single book on unnatural swellings.
quote: we have spoken elsewhere, in a single book, about swellings contrary to nature
note: This is De tumoribus praeter naturam.

title: Surgeons opening muscle swellings found only scattered air
summary: Some surgeons who cut into unnatural swellings in muscles, expecting pus, found only pneuma scattered through the flesh. Others found clots or a viscous, mucus-like fluid.
quote: some have sometimes cut into swellings contrary to nature in muscles, expecting to find pus in the depth, and then found nothing other than pneuma scattered in small portions throughout the whole flesh
note: K15.770-771 continues with the clots and mucus.

title: In Asia people call all swellings 'systrophai'
summary: Galen explains 'gatherings of diseases' by current usage: he still hears many people in 'our Asia' call all unnatural swellings systrophai.
quote: for even now I hear many people in our Asia naming in this way all the swellings contrary to nature

title: Wrestlers and pankratiasts strangled by an armlock
summary: As an example of a manifest cause of sudden voicelessness Galen gives a wrestler or pankratiast nearly strangled by an opponent's forearms locked around him.
quote: as if someone wrestling or competing in the pankration were brought into danger of being strangled from the encircling of the forearms

title: Ancients called arteries 'veins'; 'interceptions of pneumata' as pulselessness
summary: Galen notes that the ancients used sphygmoi for several kinds of throbbing and called the arteries 'veins'. So 'interceptions of pneumata along the veins' may mean pulselessness (asphyxia).
quote: for the ancients called the arteries "veins"
note: Checks verdict is 'fail'.

title: Galen bleeds at once instead of fomenting first, with rubbing
summary: Where the author fomented before venesection, Galen always cuts the inner elbow vein at once to save time. Many attendants rub the body meanwhile, and if blood will not flow he rubs and foments until it does.
quote: it is better to do what we ourselves have always written: to cut at once the inner vein at the elbow

title: Twelve to sixteen kotylai of ass's milk: customary for the ancients
summary: The appendix prescribes at least 12 kotylai of boiled ass's milk, and over 16 if the patient is strong. Galen says such quantities were customary with all the ancients. For the upward purge he would give white hellebore or another emetic.
quote: do not be surprised at the quantity of the milk, for this was customary with all the ancients.
note: 12 kotylai is about 3.3 litres.

title: Treating synanche: sublingual venesection and attractive neck plasters
summary: Treatment combines whole-body evacuation (venesection, purging, clysters), astringent and hot pungent local drugs, incision of the veins under the tongue, and attractive drugs on the neck to draw the humours outward.
quote: and, without drugs, the veins beneath the tongue, when incised, evacuate the inflammation in the pharynx

title: Inspecting the throat by depressing the tongue
summary: In the bilious kind of synanche, if the patient opens the mouth wide and the tongue is pressed down, the visible pharynx shows no swelling. The inflamed part lies out of sight.
quote: And if you bid these patients open the mouth as wide as possible and depress the tongue, in order to inspect the parts about the pharynx

title: 'He had a crisis' implies survival; deaths are specified
summary: Galen notes a usage of unqualified terms for the better case. A good crisis is called simply 'he had a crisis', but a fatal one is 'having had a crisis, he died'. Likewise 'bile' means yellow bile and 'cloudy urine' means white clouds.
quote: when the one who has had the crisis dies, they do not say it simply, but say the whole thing: 'having had a crisis, he died'

title: List of powerful critical days in acute and chronic disease
summary: Galen lists the powerful critical days: in acute diseases the 3rd, 5th, 7th, 9th, 11th, 14th and 17th, and in chronic ones the 60th and 80th, with the 20th, 34th and 40th between them.
quote: In acute diseases these are the 3rd and the 5th and 7th and 9th and 11th and 14th and 17th; in chronic ones, the 60th and 80th.
note: The numbers are Greek numeral letters in the text and could easily be corrupted.

title: Even days called 'odd' (perittai) in the critical-days list
summary: The draft says the 20th, 34th and 40th days 'too are odd', which is arithmetically false. The 14th also stands in a list of 'odd' days.
quote: Intermediate between these are the 20th and 34th and 40th, and these too are odd.
note: περιττός may mean 'remarkable or powerful' here rather than 'odd-numbered', or the numerals are corrupt. The draft's 'odd' should be checked.

title: Empirical writers generalize from one or two observations
summary: Galen charges the appendix author with writing down a 'syndrome of empirical signs' from one or two cases as if it were universal. A trained physician sees such lists as varied but useless.
quote: derived from things seen once or twice, they carry a pronouncement of universal character

title: Single cases should be recorded as in Epidemics, with name and days
summary: Galen says the author rashly generalized from a particular observation. He should have recorded it as Hippocrates did in the Epidemics, with the patient's name and the day of each event.
quote: stating first at the beginning the name of the patient and after this also the days on which each thing happened

title: Hiccup from pepper; feverish patients cured by vomiting acrid humour
summary: Galen notes that hiccup can come from something pungent biting the stomach mouth, as when someone swallows too much pepper. Some febrile patients vomited a corrosive humour and were freed of hiccup at once.
quote: as when someone swallows too much pepper or something of that kind

title: Pine-cone electuary: cone boiled with horehound, then honey
summary: Galen gives his own electuary for chest expectoration. A fresh, resinous pine cone is boiled in water with horehound, honey is added to the decoction, and it is boiled again to the thickness of honey.
quote: Boiling it fresh in water together with horehound, then mixing a moderate amount of honey into the decoction, and boiling this again to a honey-like consistency
note: The 'kokkalos' and myrrh electuary is the appendix's.

title: Kokkalos = konos (ancients) = strobilos (recent physicians)
summary: Galen notes that the pine cone the author calls kokkalos was called konos by the ancient Greeks and strobilos by nearly all recent physicians.
quote: the kokkalos spoken of by him was not so named by the ancient Greeks, but rather konos (cone), just as by nearly all the more recent physicians it is called strobilos

title: Zythos (barley beer) brewed nowadays
summary: On the 'barley water' for thirst, Galen wishes the author had said how the barley is prepared: simply soaked, or as people nowadays do when they make zythos from it.
quote: whether simply by steeping it, or as those nowadays do who make zythos from it, or in some other manner
note: This is evidence for barley beer (zythos) in Galen's day, typically Egyptian.

title: Ancient Empiricists' term syndromē; ancients said synedreuonta
summary: Galen notes that 'concurrence' (syndromē) is the ancient Empiricists' name. The ancients called such symptoms 'sitting together with' (synedreuonta) the affections.
quote: the 'concurrence' (συνδρομή), as it is named by the ancient Empiricists—though the ancients used to call such symptoms things 'sitting together with' (συνεδρεύοντα) the affections

title: Galen purged on day one, two, four or five, not by number
summary: Against the author's 'purge on the fourth day', Galen says purging must follow the state of the humours. He himself has purged on the first, second, fourth and fifth days.
quote: so that we too have purged around the first day, sometimes also on the second and the fourth, and sometimes also on the fifth

title: From experience garlic is not flatulent, no hotter than onion
summary: Judging foods by experience, Galen denies that garlic is flatulent or gives more heat than onion, especially briefly boiled. It dries and heats and, given to a prepared body, cures heaviness of the head.
quote: garlic would not rightly be said to be flatulent, nor to bring to those who have eaten it a sensation of greater heat than in the case of onion

title: Breads from emmer, einkorn, barley; peasants bake millet loaves
summary: Explaining 'cereal foods', Galen lists the grains used for bread: wheat above all, then emmer (zeia), einkorn (tiphē) and barley. Country people even make loaves from millet.
quote: zeia (emmer) and [876] tiphe (einkorn) and barley; and country people make loaves even from millet

title: Some say chickpea's 'flatulence' means it distends the genitals
summary: Galen reports that some interpreters read the chickpea's flatulence as distending the genitals. He refers the 'pain' instead to pain from inflation.
quote: Some write that the chickpea is flatulent for this reason, as distending the genitals
note: This alludes to the chickpea's reputed aphrodisiac effect.

title: Goats are best in summer from feeding on tree shoots
summary: Goat meat is best in summer and worst in autumn. Galen explains that goats then feed on the shoots and stalks of trees, which are plentiful in late spring and summer.
quote: for goats the most suitable nourishment is the shoots and stalks of trees, which they have in abundance at the end of spring and during the summer

title: Foxes and the beccafico taste best in autumn from grapes
summary: To show that diet shapes meat quality, Galen notes that foxes have their finest flesh in autumn from eating grapes. The small bird called sykalis (beccafico) is likewise finest then.
quote: you can learn also from foxes, which in autumn especially have the finest flesh on account of the grapes

title: Homer's suitors: fattened hogs and blood-stuffed goat stomachs
summary: Galen quotes Homer on piglets (choiroi) for servants and fattened hogs for the suitors. He mocks the suitors as undiscerning eaters who also ate goat stomachs stuffed with blood and fat, the hardest food to digest.
quote: just as also in their eating the stomachs of goats stuffed with blood and fat, than which what food could you find harder to digest?
note: The lines are from Odyssey 14.80-81, and the goat-stomach sausages from Odyssey 18 and 20.

title: Three kinds of dropsy; ascites tapped by paracentesis
summary: Galen distinguishes ascites (thin fluid below the thorax, sometimes drained by tapping), tympanias (full of air) and hyposarkidios (phlegm throughout the body). Some physicians wrongly posit four kinds.
quote: of the dropsies one kind gathers a quantity of fluid that is thin in consistency in the whole region below the thorax, and by tapping this we sometimes evacuate the fluid

title: Venesection only for anasarca from suppressed haemorrhoids or menses
summary: Only the dropsy throughout the flesh sometimes needs phlebotomy at its start, when it began from suppressed haemorrhoids, suppressed menses or plethora. No one has dared bleed tympanites or ascites.
quote: when at any rate it is formed having begun from a suppression of a haemorrhoid, or of the menses in women

title: Dioscorides' edition read 'spring' instead of 'summer'
summary: Galen reports that Dioscorides and others wrote 'the spring season' instead of 'summer' in the dropsy passage. They feared summer would dissolve the faculty and winter would add chill.
quote: Some people, however, like Dioscorides, wrote not 'the summer season' but 'the spring'
note: This is Dioscorides the Hippocratic editor (Hadrianic era), not the pharmacologist.

title: Young wines are never tawny
summary: Galen calls the author's diet of hot bread in dark wine and oil 'layman's and archaic', because dark wine makes melancholic blood. Tawny, thin, older wine is better, since no young wine is tawny.
quote: for of young wines none will be tawny, but either white or red or dark, whereas as they age they become both tawny and yellow

title: Exertions are occasions (prophaseis), not causes, of disease
summary: Running, wrestling, sex, chilling and the like only expose a disease the body is already close to. Alone they cause at most an ephemeral fever, so Galen calls them occasions rather than causes.
quote: each of such things becomes not the cause of the disease but its occasion

title: 'Up in the air' (meteōros): current slang for absent-minded
summary: Galen says the author was either forgetful or 'such a person as the one nowadays called by most people up in the air' (meteōros).
quote: and such a person as the one nowadays called by most people 'up in the air'

title: Cantharides drink for dropsy (appendix)
summary: The appendix prescribes three blister beetles with head, feet and wings removed, ground in three kyathoi of water and drunk fasting, followed by a warm bath and oil-bread.
quote: Three cantharides: having removed the head of each and the feet and wings, having ground the bodies in three kyathoi of water
note: This is the Hippocratic lemma; Galen's response is the case at K15.913.

title: Bold physician's cantharides trials: two dropsical patients died
summary: A daring physician followed the cantharides recipe. His patient formed an abscess in the calf that he incised, water poured out, and the man died some days later. Told to give heads, feet and wings instead, he did so for another patient, who died the same way.
quote: A certain bold physician, having read this passage, removed the aforesaid parts of the cantharides and gave them to a dropsical patient
note: Galen adds that some have used a diuretic drug made from cantharides without harm.

title: Eyelid trichiasis surgery called anabrochismos
summary: Galen summarizes the appendix's closing prescriptions and names its suture operation for ingrowing eyelashes: anabrochismos.
quote: next he wrote the surgical procedure for hairs on the eyelids, which they call anabrochismos
note: The Greek spelling here is ἀναβρογχισμόν (with gamma), a variant of ἀναβροχισμός.

title: Irritations that weaken: worms rising to the stomach, nocturnal itching
summary: Under 'irritation' Galen includes biting humours, sleeplessness, anger, grief, worms that have climbed from the intestines into the stomach, and itching of the skin at night.
quote: certain worms that have ascended from the intestines to the stomach, and itching of the whole skin or even of certain parts, setting in during the night

title: Akraton ('unmixed') in the Greek; draft renders 'of no avail'
summary: The Greek says melikraton's slight cleansing power is ἄκρατον ('unmixed'), which makes no sense. The draft silently renders 'of no avail', as if reading ἄπρακτον.
quote: This slight smegmatic quality of melikraton, then, is of no avail (ἄκρατον) not because it is smegmatic, but because it is slight
note: The text is probably corrupt (ἄπρακτον or ἀχρεῖον?). The draft's rendering is reasonable but unsignalled.

title: 'Work of swiftness' in peristalsis passage looks corrupt
summary: The draft says it is 'the work of swiftness' to thrust contents away. This does not fit the argument about the direction of peristaltic movement.
quote: and it is the work of swiftness (ταχύτητος) to thrust away the contents from those parts in which they are contained
note: Perhaps the text should read something like 'of the contraction' (συστολῆς?). The draft keeps the transmitted word literally.

title: 'Meta tēn kephalēn' rendered 'in the region of the head'
summary: The draft renders μετὰ τὴν κεφαλήν as 'in the region of the head'. With the accusative μετά normally means 'after', so κατὰ τὴν κεφαλήν is probably the right reading.
quote: which either has its local origin in the region of the head (μετὰ τὴν κεφαλὴν), or is carried up from below
note: The draft translates the sense correctly, but the text needs emending.

title: Garbled clause on grass-eating animals in the goat-meat passage
summary: The draft's 'even as (καθάπερ) the grass-eating animals are bad' breaks the argument about why goat meat is best in summer. The sentence looks corrupt or mistranslated.
quote: even as (καθάπερ) the grass-eating animals are bad, because they no longer have the grass green
note: The intended contrast is probably that grazers are worse in summer when the grass dries, while goats are better.
